concepts: Determinant and adjoint of a matrix
question: Let $J_{n,m}=\int_0^{1/2}\frac{x^n}{x^m-1}\,dx$, $\forall\, n>m$ and $n,m\in\mathbb{N}$. Consider a matrix $A=[a_{ij}]_{3\times3}$ where $a_{ij}=\begin{cases}J_{6+i,3}-J_{i+3,3}, & i\le j\\ 0, & i>j\end{cases}$. Then $|\mathrm{adj}\,A^{-1}|$ is:
key_idea: $x^{6+i}-x^{3+i}=x^{3+i}(x^3-1)$ cancels the denominator, so $a_{ij}=\int_0^{1/2}x^{3+i}dx$ depends on the row only.
solution: So $a_{ij}=\frac{1}{(4+i)2^{4+i}}$ for $i\le j$ and $0$ for $i>j$: the entries of row $1$ are $\frac{1}{5\cdot2^5}$, of row $2$ (from column 2) $\frac{1}{6\cdot2^6}$, of row $3$ (column 3) $\frac{1}{7\cdot2^7}$.
The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries: $|A|=\frac{1}{5\cdot2^5}\cdot\frac{1}{6\cdot2^6}\cdot\frac{1}{7\cdot2^7}$.
useful_results: $J_{n+m,m}-J_{n,m}=\int x^n dx$, because $x^{n+m}-x^n=x^n(x^m-1)$; so a difference of two such integrals with the same $m$ never needs partial fractions. Check: $J_{7,3}-J_{4,3}=\int_0^{1/2}x^4dx=\frac{1}{5\cdot2^5}$.
For an $n\times n$ matrix $M$: $|\mathrm{adj}\,M|=|M|^{n-1}$ and $\mathrm{adj}(M^{-1})=\frac{M}{|M|}$; for $n=3$, $|\mathrm{adj}\,A^{-1}|=|A|^{-2}$.
The determinant of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix is the product of its diagonal entries, whatever lies above the diagonal.
Entries that depend on one index only (here $a_{ij}=c_i$ for $j\ge i$) give a triangular matrix whose determinant is $c_1c_2c_3$.

concepts: Definite integral equation with a separable kernel
question: The function $f(x)$, that satisfies the condition $f(x)=x+\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\cdot\cos y\,f(y)\,dy$, is:
key_idea: $\sin x$ comes out of the $y$-integral, so $f(x)=x+A\sin x$ with a constant $A=\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos y\,f(y)\,dy$ to be found.
solution: $\sin x$ does not depend on $y$, so $f(x)=x+\sin x\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos y\,f(y)\,dy$.
$A=\left[y\sin y+\cos y\right]_0^{\pi/2}+\frac A2\left[-\frac{\cos2y}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2}$ (the first integral is by parts).

alternate_solutions.idea: Rank-one kernel: $A\left(1-\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin y\cos y\,dy\right)=\int_0^{\pi/2}y\cos y\,dy$, with the last integral read off from the area under the inverse function.
solution: As before $f=x+A\sin x$ and $A=\int_0^{\pi/2}y\cos y\,dy+A\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin y\cos y\,dy$.
The curve $u=\sin y$ splits the rectangle $[0,1]\times[0,\frac\pi2]$ into two regions: $\int_0^1\sin^{-1}u\,du+\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin y\,dy=1\cdot\frac\pi2$.

useful_results: Separable kernel: if $f(x)=g(x)+p(x)\int_a^bq(y)f(y)\,dy$, then $f=g+A\,p$ with $A=\frac{\int_a^b q\,g}{1-\int_a^b q\,p}$ (needs $\int qp\ne1$). Here $q=\cos,\ g=x,\ p=\sin$: $A=\frac{\pi/2-1}{1-1/2}=\pi-2$.
If $\int_a^b q\,p=1$ the equation is singular: it has either no solution or infinitely many, so always check the denominator $1-\int qp$.
Inverse-function area: for increasing $f$, $\int_a^bf(x)dx+\int_{f(a)}^{f(b)}f^{-1}(u)du=b f(b)-a f(a)$. Check: $f=\sin$ on $[0,\frac\pi2]$ gives $1+\left(\frac\pi2-1\right)=\frac\pi2$.
Standard values: $\int_0^{\pi/2}y\cos y\,dy=\frac\pi2-1$ and $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin y\cos y\,dy=\frac12$.

concepts: Definite integral of greatest integer and modulus functions
question: Let $[t]$ denote the greatest integer $\le t$. Then the value of $8\cdot\int_{-1/2}^{1}\big([2x]+|x|\big)dx$ is ______.
key_idea: Split at the points where $[2x]$ jumps ($x=0,\frac12$) and where $|x|$ changes form ($x=0$).
solution: On $\left[-\frac12,1\right]$: $[2x]=-1$ for $-\frac12\le x<0$, $[2x]=0$ for $0\le x<\frac12$, $[2x]=1$ for $\frac12\le x<1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $[2x]=2x-\{2x\}$: the fractional part averages $\frac12$ over each full period, and $\int|x|$ is a sum of two triangle areas.
solution: The interval $\left[-\frac12,1\right]$ has length $\frac32$, i.e. exactly $3$ periods, so $\int_{-1/2}^{1}\{2x\}dx=3\cdot\frac14=\frac34$.
$\int_{-1/2}^{1}|x|dx$ is the area of two right isosceles triangles with legs $\frac12$ and $1$: $\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12+\frac12\cdot1\cdot1=\frac18+\frac12=\frac58$.

useful_results: $[kx]=kx-\{kx\}$, and $\{kx\}$ has period $\frac1k$ with mean $\frac12$: $\int_0^{n/k}\{kx\}dx=\frac{n}{2k}$ for integer $n$. Check: $k=2,n=3$ gives $\frac34$.
For integers $a<b$: $\int_a^b[x]dx=\sum_{k=a}^{b-1}k$; e.g. $\int_0^3[x]dx=0+1+2=3$.
$\int_{-p}^{q}|x|dx=\frac{p^2+q^2}{2}$ for $p,q\ge0$. Here $p=\frac12,q=1$ gives $\frac58$.

For any integral with a greatest-integer function, split at every point where its argument crosses an integer, and use $\int_a^b[x]dx=\int_a^bx\,dx-\int_a^b\{x\}dx$ over whole periods when the length is a whole number.

question: Let $g:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function such that $\int\left(\frac{x(\cos x-\sin x)}{e^x+1}+\frac{g(x)\left(e^x+1-xe^x\right)}{\left(e^x+1\right)^2}\right)dx=\frac{x\,g(x)}{e^x+1}+c$, for all $x>0$, where $c$ is an arbitrary constant. Then:
key_idea: Differentiating both sides makes every $g$-term cancel and leaves $g'(x)=\cos x-\sin x$.
solution: Differentiate both sides w.r.t. $x$: $\frac{x(\cos x-\sin x)}{e^x+1}+\frac{g(e^x+1-xe^x)}{(e^x+1)^2}=\frac{(e^x+1)(g+xg')-e^x\cdot x\cdot g}{(e^x+1)^2}$.
The $g$-terms on the two sides are equal ($g(e^x+1)-xe^xg$ each), so they cancel and $(e^x+1)\,x(\cos x-\sin x)=(e^x+1)\,x\,g'$.
Hence $g'(x)=\cos x-\sin x$, and $g(x)=\sin x+\cos x+C$.
(A) On $\left(0,\frac\pi4\right)$, $g'=\cos x-\sin x>0$, so $g$ is increasing; (A) is false.
(B) $g''(x)=-\sin x-\cos x<0$ on $\left(0,\frac\pi4\right)$, so $g'$ is decreasing; (B) is false.
(C) Let $h=g+g'=2\cos x+C$. Then $h'=g'+g''=-2\sin x<0$ on $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$, so $h$ is decreasing; (C) is false.
(D) Let $\phi=g-g'=2\sin x+C$. Then $\phi'=g'-g''=2\cos x>0$ on $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$, so $g-g'$ is increasing; (D) is true.

alternate_solutions.idea: Spot the product rule: the integrand is $(\cos x-\sin x)\,u+g\,u'$ with $u=\frac{x}{e^x+1}$, and write $g$ as a shifted sine to test the options.
solution: The integrand is $(\cos x-\sin x)\,u+g\,u'$, because $\frac{x(\cos x-\sin x)}{e^x+1}=(\cos x-\sin x)\,u$.
The given identity says the integrand equals $(g\,u)'=g'u+g\,u'$.
Subtract: $\left(g'-(\cos x-\sin x)\right)u=0$. Since $u>0$ for $x>0$, $g'=\cos x-\sin x=\sqrt2\cos\left(x+\frac\pi4\right)$.
On $\left(0,\frac\pi4\right)$, $\theta\in\left(\frac\pi4,\frac\pi2\right)$: $\cos\theta>0$ so $g$ increases (A false), and $\cos\theta$ decreases so $g'$ decreases (B false).

useful_results: If $\int F\,dx=u(x)\,g(x)+c$ with unknown $g$, then $F=u'g+u\,g'$: compare with $F$ to cancel the $g$-terms and isolate $g'$. Valid wherever $u\ne0$.
$a\cos x+b\sin x=R\sin(x+\varphi)$ with $R=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$; for $g=\sin x+\cos x+C$: $g+g'=2\cos x+C$ and $g-g'=2\sin x+C$ (check: at $x=0$, $g+g'=1+1+C$ ✓).
For $g=\sin x+\cos x$: $g''=-g$ up to the constant $C$, so $g'$ increases exactly where $g''=-(g-C)\ge0$, i.e. where $\sin x+\cos x\le0$; never on $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$.
Monotonicity of a combination $g\pm g'$ is decided by the sign of $g'\pm g''$; compute it directly rather than comparing graphs.

question: If $\int\frac1x\sqrt{\frac{1-x}{1+x}}\,dx=g(x)+c$, $g(1)=0$, then $g\left(\frac12\right)$ is equal to:
correction_note: The PDF's second line is garbled: it writes $\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos\theta}{1+\sin\theta}}$ (should be $\frac{1-\cos\theta}{1+\cos\theta}$) and a stray 'x - sinθ dx' (should be $dx=-\sin\theta\,d\theta$). It also stops at $\frac\pi3+\ln(2-\sqrt3)$ without matching the option form $\ln\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt3+1}$. Corrected the typos and added the last matching step. The answer (A) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Rationalise: $\sqrt{\frac{1-x}{1+x}}=\frac{1-x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ splits the integrand into two standard integrals.

useful_results: For $\sqrt{\frac{a-x}{a+x}}$ or $\sqrt{\frac{a+x}{a-x}}$ either put $x=a\cos2\theta$ (or $a\cos\theta$) or multiply by the conjugate: $\sqrt{\frac{a-x}{a+x}}=\frac{a-x}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}$.
$\int\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{1-x^2}}=-\ln\frac{1+\sqrt{1-x^2}}{|x|}+c$ for $0<|x|<1$; and $\int\sec\theta\,d\theta=\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|+c$.
$\tan\frac\theta2=\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos\theta}{1+\cos\theta}}=\frac{1-\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$ for $\theta\in(0,\pi)$.
Conjugate pairs: $\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt3+1}=2-\sqrt3=\frac{1}{2+\sqrt3}$; remember when matching log options.

concepts: Integrals of the form e^x [f(x) + f'(x)]
question: If $\int\frac{\left(x^2+1\right)e^x}{(x+1)^2}\,dx=f(x)\,e^x+C$, where $C$ is a constant, then $\frac{d^3f}{dx^3}$ at $x=1$ is equal to:
key_idea: Split the rational factor into pieces of the form $\varphi+\varphi'$ so that $\int e^x(\varphi+\varphi')dx=e^x\varphi$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Subtract $(x+1)^2$ from the numerator: $x^2+1=(x+1)^2-2x$, giving $f=1-\frac{2}{x+1}$ at once and an immediate third derivative.
solution: Let $\varphi=-\frac{2}{x+1}$; then $\varphi'=\frac{2}{(x+1)^2}$, so the integrand is $e^x\cdot1+e^x(\varphi+\varphi')$.
$\int e^xdx=e^x$ and $\int e^x(\varphi+\varphi')dx=e^x\varphi$, so the integral is $e^x\left(1-\frac{2}{x+1}\right)+C$.

useful_results: $\int e^x\left[\varphi(x)+\varphi'(x)\right]dx=e^x\varphi(x)+C$ for any differentiable $\varphi$. Check: $\int e^x\left(\frac1x-\frac1{x^2}\right)dx=\frac{e^x}{x}$ since $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{e^x}{x}=e^x\left(\frac1x-\frac1{x^2}\right)$.
More generally $\int e^{ax}\left[a\varphi+\varphi'\right]dx=e^{ax}\varphi+C$.

Recognition cue: $e^x\times$ (rational function with denominator a power of $x+1$): rewrite the numerator in powers of $(x+1)$ so terms pair as $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$, with any leftover pure $e^x$ integrated separately.

concepts: Definite integration: King property and symmetry
question: The value of the integral $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{(1+e^x)(\sin^6x+\cos^6x)}$ is equal to:
key_idea: Pairing $x$ with $-x$ turns $\frac{1}{1+e^x}$ into $\frac{e^x}{1+e^x}$; the two add to $1$ and the factor $1+e^x$ disappears.

alternate_solutions.idea: After removing $1+e^x$, put $t=\tan x$ to get $\frac{1+t^2}{t^4-t^2+1}$ and use $u=t-\frac1t$ (the symmetric-in-$t,\frac1t$ trick).
solution: As in the primary solution, pairing $x$ with $-x$ gives $I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{\sin^6x+\cos^6x}$.

useful_results: $\int_{-a}^{a}\frac{f(x)}{1+e^{kx}}dx=\int_0^af(x)dx$ for even $f$ and any real $k\ne0$ (pair $x$ with $-x$). Check: $f=1,a=1,k=1$: $\int_{-1}^1\frac{dx}{1+e^x}=1$.
$\sin^6x+\cos^6x=1-\frac34\sin^22x=\frac{5+3\cos4x}{8}$ and $\sin^4x+\cos^4x=1-\frac12\sin^22x$.
$\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1-k\sin^22x}=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{1-k}}$ for $0\le k<1$. Check: $k=\frac34$ gives $\pi$; $k=\frac12$ gives $\frac{\pi}{\sqrt2}=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{\sin^4x+\cos^4x}$.
If $F\left(\frac\pi2-x\right)=F(x)$ then $\int_0^{\pi/2}F=2\int_0^{\pi/4}F$; and $u=t-\frac1t$ handles integrands of the form $\frac{1+t^{-2}}{\text{poly in }t^2+t^{-2}}$.

concepts: Limit of a sum as a definite integral
question: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n^2}{(n^2+1)(n+1)}+\frac{n^2}{(n^2+4)(n+2)}+\dots+\frac{n^2}{(n^2+n^2)(n+n)}\right)$ is equal to:
key_idea: Divide each term by $n^3$ to get $\frac1n F\left(\frac rn\right)$ with $F(x)=\frac{1}{(1+x^2)(1+x)}$, so the limit is $\int_0^1F$.
solution: Divide numerator and denominator by $n^3$: $T_r=\frac{1}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{\left(1+\frac{r^2}{n^2}\right)\left(1+\frac rn\right)}$.
The sum $\sum_{r=1}^{n}T_r$ is a Riemann sum, so the limit is $\int_0^1\frac{dx}{(1+x^2)(1+x)}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: After the Riemann step, substitute $x=\tan\theta$ so that $1+x^2$ is absorbed by $dx$, leaving $\int\frac{d\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$ (split numerator as half the denominator plus half its derivative).
solution: The Riemann-sum step is as before: the limit is $I=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{(1+x^2)(1+x)}$.

useful_results: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{r=1}^{n}F\left(\frac rn\right)=\int_0^1F(x)dx$ for continuous $F$ (for $r=0$ to $n-1$ the limit is the same).
Recognition cue: a term $\frac{n^2}{(n^2+r^2)(n+r)}$ has total degree $n^{-1}$ after cancelling, so it is $\frac1n F\left(\frac rn\right)$; divide by the highest power of $n$ in each factor.
$\int\frac{dx}{(1+x)(1+x^2)}=\frac12\ln(1+x)-\frac14\ln(1+x^2)+\frac12\tan^{-1}x+C$.
$\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{d\theta}{1+\tan\theta}=\frac\pi8+\frac14\ln2$, whereas $\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{d\theta}{1+\tan\theta}=\frac\pi4$ (King property).

question: The value of $\int_0^\pi\frac{e^{\cos x}\sin x}{\left(1+\cos^2x\right)\left(e^{\cos x}+e^{-\cos x}\right)}dx$ is equal to:
key_idea: $x\to\pi-x$ flips $\cos x$ to $-\cos x$, so $\frac{e^{c}}{e^c+e^{-c}}$ and $\frac{e^{-c}}{e^c+e^{-c}}$ add to $1$.
solution: King property $x\to\pi-x$ ($\cos\to-\cos$, $\sin\to\sin$): $I=\int_0^\pi\frac{e^{-\cos x}\sin x}{(1+\cos^2x)(e^{-\cos x}+e^{\cos x})}dx$ ... (2).
Add (1) and (2): the numerators $e^{\cos x}+e^{-\cos x}$ cancel the common factor, so $2I=\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx$.
The integrand is symmetric about $\frac\pi2$: $2I=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx$, so $I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $t=\cos x$ at once, split $\frac{e^t}{e^t+e^{-t}}=\frac12+\frac12\tanh t$ and kill the odd part.
solution: $\frac{\tanh t}{1+t^2}$ is odd, so the second integral is $0$.

useful_results: For $p>0$: $\frac{p(t)}{p(t)+p(-t)}=\frac12+\text{(odd function)}$, so $\int_{-a}^{a}E(t)\frac{p(t)}{p(t)+p(-t)}dt=\frac12\int_{-a}^{a}E(t)dt$ for even $E$. Here $p=e^t$.
$\int_0^\pi f(\cos x)\sin x\,dx=\int_{-1}^{1}f(t)dt$; and $x\to\pi-x$ sends $\cos x$ to $-\cos x$, $\sin x$ unchanged.
$\frac{e^t}{e^t+e^{-t}}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-2t}}$ is the logistic function $\sigma(2t)$, with $\sigma(s)+\sigma(-s)=1$.
King property: $\int_a^bf(x)dx=\int_a^bf(a+b-x)dx$; use it when $f(x)+f(a+b-x)$ simplifies (here to $\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}$).

question: If $b_n=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^2nx}{\sin x}dx$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, then:
options: $b_3-b_2,\ b_4-b_3,\ b_5-b_4$ are in an A.P. with common difference $-2$
$\frac{1}{b_3-b_2},\ \frac{1}{b_4-b_3},\ \frac{1}{b_5-b_4}$ are in an A.P. with common difference $2$
$\frac{1}{b_3-b_2},\ \frac{1}{b_4-b_3},\ \frac{1}{b_5-b_4}$ are in an A.P. with common difference $-2$
answer: (D) $\frac{1}{b_3-b_2},\frac{1}{b_4-b_3},\frac{1}{b_5-b_4}$ are in an A.P. with common difference $-2$
key_idea: Form $b_n-b_{n-1}$ first: $\cos^2nx-\cos^2(n-1)x=-\sin x\,\sin(2n-1)x$ cancels the $\sin x$ in the denominator.
solution: Use $\cos^2A-\cos^2B=-\sin(A+B)\sin(A-B)$ with $A=nx,\ B=(n-1)x$: the numerator is $\sin(2n-1)x\,\sin(-x)$.
$\frac{1}{b_n-b_{n-1}}=-(2n-1)=-2n+1$, so for $n=3,4,5$ the reciprocals are $-5,-7,-9$: an A.P. with common difference $-2$.

The differences themselves, $-\frac15,-\frac17,-\frac19$, are neither in A.P. ($-\frac{2}{35}\ne-\frac{2}{63}$) nor in G.P. ($\frac57\ne\frac79$), so (A), (C) are false and (B) has the wrong sign; (D) is correct.
Remark: each $b_n$ alone diverges at $x=0$ (integrand $\to\infty$), but the combined integrand of $b_n-b_{n-1}$ is bounded, so the difference is a proper integral.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\frac{\sin^2nx}{\sin x}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sin(2k-1)x$ to write $b_n$ as an $n$-independent term minus the partial sum $1+\frac13+\dots+\frac1{2n-1}$.
solution: $\cos^2nx=1-\sin^2nx$, so $b_n=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{\sin x}-\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2nx}{\sin x}dx$; the first part does not depend on $n$ and cancels in any difference.
The reciprocals $\frac{1}{b_n-b_{n-1}}=1-2n$ ($=-5,-7,-9$ for $n=3,4,5$) form an A.P. with common difference $-2$: option (D).

useful_results: $\cos^2A-\cos^2B=\sin^2B-\sin^2A=-\sin(A+B)\sin(A-B)$. Check: $A=2,B=1$: both sides $\approx-0.1187$.
$\frac{\sin^2nx}{\sin x}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sin(2k-1)x$, hence $\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2nx}{\sin x}dx=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{1}{2k-1}$ (check $n=3$: $1+\frac13+\frac15=\frac{23}{15}$).
For integrals $I_n$ depending on a parameter, look at $I_n-I_{n-1}$ first: product-to-sum identities usually cancel a troublesome denominator (and any divergent common part).
$\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin(mx)dx=\frac{1-\cos(m\pi/2)}{m}$; for odd $m$ it equals $\frac1m$.
Test for sequences: A.P. iff consecutive differences are equal; G.P. iff consecutive ratios are equal; for $a_n=-\frac{1}{2n-1}$ neither holds, but $\frac1{a_n}$ is an A.P.
